chapter_title: The Chapter of the Man who asks: Why [am] I someti
spiritual_reading:
Sometimes the inner person is held in quiet concord, because the understanding is turned to what builds and the truths that have been learned are arranged in right order. Then the life of use proceeds evenly, and teaching goes forth to others in a gentle form; the will rests, the understanding rejoices in enlightened perception, and even the outer life feels unburdened because the interior is in wisdom and genuine knowing.

Yet there are times when that same person is seized by unrest. Truths lose their order, and obscurity increases with a swarm of contrary affections—resentment, grief, anger, envy, and craving. Then there is a struggle to subject these things, but at that moment no power of understanding is found that can bring them into obedience, for they surge up and press. Perverse persuasions and evil intentions then come into action and torment the mind, so that nothing in them is coherent or distinctly formed. It becomes uncertain whether such disorder is being disclosed for the sake of seeing it, or whether it has entered from without and been driven into the inner life; it is also uncertain whether it has awakened from one’s own proprium and risen in rebellion. Only this is clearly perceived: that the whole arrangement of thought is thrown into confusion. Then uses are performed without right aim, teaching loses its weight and truth in expression, and one becomes an occasion of trouble and obscurity to those conjoined in charity. Even the outer life reacts against the inner disorder, and the natural degree falls into a state of infirmity for that period.

You ask rightly about this state, and the matter can be made clear. When the inner person is joined to the outer and the enlightened understanding is received, then by the power of wisdom in obedience the mind is purified; the life is cleansed and made new in form. In that renewal there is no unrest, no confusion, no disturbance, because higher order rules the lower.

But when disturbance arises and a person is troubled, the unrest enters first through the fixed tendencies of the natural life and the compulsions that press from hereditary and acquired patterns, by which the person is stirred and vexed into craving, anger, heaviness, and grief, according to the inclination that is then chosen. Moreover, insofar as that inclination invites it, influences from the spiritual environment also trouble the person through the points of attachment by which the mind is conjoined to such influx.

Again, there are times when those higher influences are quiet and do not press, yet disorder still comes in by what is taken into the natural life and made one with it. Then irritations and confusions increase again, and anger and craving multiply with heaviness and grief, because what is admitted into the life is mingled with impure and contentious elements. These enter into the outer life together with what is appropriated, and they join themselves to the existing evils and falsities there; thus they transmit into the mind the anger and craving, the heaviness and grief, as bodily-originated thoughts and impulses.

But there are also times when what is admitted into the life is clean and rightly ordered, having more of what is living and enlightened within it and less of what is dead and harmful; then evil influence is diminished. In such a state even the surrounding natural condition becomes still, as the outer degree is clarified, and the inner form is quieted from disturbance. Peace increases through the good that is made one with the person, and one is found at ease and tranquil because the inner dwellings are better governed by the living element that then predominates through the illumination of those who are in a state of justification and completed use. In them the demand of guilt is ended, and the inner life is unburdened because it is conjoined with living goods and truths present in the person. Therefore these calm states are found within, and they pass through without causing trouble; the outer life flourishes, works become determinate and well constructed in that same order, truths are restored to their places, teaching proceeds rightly, and the inner life is free, rising into higher thought.

This is the settling of the matter you asked about: from where the bitter intentions and disorderly reasonings arise that trouble, and from where the good intentions and gentle ordered truths arise when the understanding is quiet. When the outer degree is agitated, trouble is induced through lower avenues, by impure elements admitted and appropriated in the natural life. But when the higher avenues are quiet, what is appropriated is also clear and pure; then the will is found set in right order, and the counsels of the mind rest in peace without disturbance.

fills.notes: The peaceful state describes orderly doctrine flowing into orderly use. The gap must express unimpeded execution of works from an ordered mind: ‘straightway in my works’ preserves the impersonal, causal register (order within → order in deeds).

In the opposite state, the spiritual sense demands uses done without right aim and under disorder. ‘Error and disturbance’ matches the described incoherence of counsels and the later contrast with ‘well constructed’ works.

fills.fill: to be at peace in my heart
fills.notes: The passage turns from worthless speech to inability to recover an interior state of order. The demanded complement is the loss of peace: not finding how ‘to be at peace in my heart’, which also echoes ¶2’s opening state and keeps the substrate’s interior-causality focus.

The disturbance is said to enter ‘first through’ natal and stellar determinations; correspondentially this is influx through fixed natural tendencies. ‘In many ways’ suits the layered avenues of influx without importing later institutional terms.

The stars are agents that ‘turn over him and stir him’. The missing verb must express oppressive compulsion from above into the natural degree. ‘Press upon him’ fits the causal sequence (birth-signs and difficult stars that press upon him, then stir and trouble).

The structure contrasts two causes: (a) heavenly powers tranquil, yet (b) trouble comes by nourishment. The gap needs a hinge introducing a different avenue while maintaining tranquillity above: ‘another way; though’.

The context lists vehicles of intake: nourishment eaten, then ‘or else indeed in some … or in the water’. A ‘mixture’ fits the correspondential idea of impure elements entering via ingestion, without moralizing. ‘Herbs’ keeps a natural, impersonal register as a common carrier of qualities.
Here the nourishment is ‘pure’ and therefore ordered: more light and life, less waste. ‘Well blended’ conveys right composition (order of parts) rather than later ethical language.

The atmosphere above becoming still is explained as purification through its finer elements. ‘Air’ and ‘wind’ keep the oldest cosmological register: surrounding mediums correspond to the natural degree being clarified.

After ‘the image is calmed from …’ the next clause is ‘… increases in you through those good parts’. The missing sequence must remove agitation and introduce the resulting state. ‘Every disturbance; and peace’ matches the spiritual sense: quieted from disturbance, then peace increases.

This closes the ordered-state description: doctrines in order ‘as your words …’. The spiritual sense demands teaching proceeding rightly and gently. ‘Sweet in your mouth’ echoes ¶2’s ‘sweetness’ and keeps the impersonal correspondence (ordered truth → sweet utterance).

‘Their dues have ceased, while their soul is carefree … they have been allied…’ The causal link required by the spiritual sense is that carefreeness is due to conjunction. ‘Because’ supplies the needed relation without adding later doctrinal framing.

assessment: Most gaps are constrained by the chapter’s strict correspondence chain: inner order produces sweet teaching and determinate works; disorder produces confused counsels and sickening of the outer degree; disturbance enters by fixed natal inclinations, by heavenly attachments, and by impure intake; peace increases by pure, well-ordered intake and a stilled surrounding medium. A few noun-level details (notably the specific ‘mixture’ in ¶8 and the exact atmospheric phrase in ¶10) remain tentative because the spiritual sense fixes function more tightly than surface imagery.
